title: Create Maximum Number
description: Brute force to optimized: enumerating every subsequence pair and interleaving versus a monotonic-stack max subsequence, greedy suffix-comparison merge, and exhaustive split search.

blocks.text: 1. Problem Statement

Problem Summary: Given two arrays of single-digit numbers, nums1 and nums2, and an integer k, create the maximum number of length k by choosing a subsequence from each array (preserving relative order within each), then merging (interleaving) them together (preserving the relative order of digits from each original array). Return this maximum number as an array of digits.

blocks.text: 2. Pattern Detection

blocks.content: {"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["\"Choose a subsequence of a given length, maximizing its value\"","A monotonic stack, similar to Remove K Digits, greedily discards smaller earlier digits when a larger one appears"],["\"Merge two sequences preserving order, maximizing the combined result\"","A greedy merge comparing entire remaining suffixes, not just the next digit, to decide which sequence to take from next"]]}

blocks.text: 3. Understand the Problem

This problem combines three separate subroutines: (1) given an array and a target length, find its lexicographically largest subsequence of that length using a monotonic stack; (2) given two digit sequences, greedily merge them into the largest possible combined sequence; (3) try every way to split k between the two arrays (i digits from nums1, k-i from nums2), keeping the best overall result.

blocks.title: Analogy: Combining the Best Selections from Two Card Decks Into the Highest-Value Hand
blocks.text: Picture picking a fixed number of cards from EACH of two decks (keeping their relative order within each deck), then interleaving the two selections together (preserving each deck's internal order) to form the highest possible combined hand. This requires deciding how many cards to take from each deck, choosing the best subsequence from each, and then merging them optimally.

blocks.caption: Try every split of k between the two arrays; for each split, find the best subsequence from each and merge them optimally

blocks.text: 4. Understand with Examples
Result: [9, 8, 6, 5, 3]. Taking [6,5] from nums1 and [9,8,3] from nums2, merged as [9,8,6,5,3], gives the maximum length-5 number.
5. How Should We Think?

Before trying every possible way to choose and interleave digits, notice the problem decomposes cleanly into three independently-solvable pieces: finding the best subsequence of a given length from ONE array (a monotonic stack problem), merging two ALREADY-chosen sequences optimally (a greedy merge problem comparing full remaining suffixes), and trying every valid split of k between the two arrays.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: For a SINGLE array and a target length, the largest subsequence of that length is found by a monotonic stack: scan left to right, popping smaller digits off the stack (as long as enough digits remain to still reach the target length) whenever a larger digit arrives.

Observation 2: Given two ALREADY-chosen digit sequences to merge (preserving each one's internal order), the greedy choice at each step is to take from whichever sequence is LEXICOGRAPHICALLY GREATER starting from its current position, comparing full remaining suffixes (not just the next single digit), since a tie on the next digit could be broken by what follows.

Observation 3: Since the split of k between the two arrays (how many digits come from nums1 versus nums2) is not given, every valid split (from max(0, k-nums2.length) to min(k, nums1.length)) must be tried, keeping the overall best merged result.

Observation 4: Combining these three pieces, for each split: extract the best subsequence of that length from each array, merge them greedily, and compare against the best result found so far.

This leads to trying every valid split of k between the two arrays; for each split, extracting the maximum subsequence of the required length from each array via a monotonic stack, then greedily merging the two subsequences (comparing full remaining suffixes at each step) to form the combined candidate, keeping the best across all splits.
6. Brute Force Solution
Try every possible pair of subsequences (one from each array, of any lengths summing to k), and every possible way to interleave them, tracking the maximum result found.
Step by step algorithm

items: Enumerate every possible subsequence of nums1 and every possible subsequence of nums2 whose combined length equals k.
For each such pair, enumerate every possible way to interleave them while preserving each one's internal order.
Track the maximum resulting number across all these combinations.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Enumerating every subsequence pair and every interleaving directly explores every possible result, guaranteed correct.
This is combinatorially explosive: choosing subsequences alone is exponential in array length, and interleavings multiply this further.

blocks.text: 7. Analyze the Brute Force

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: exponential (combinatorial explosion from both subsequence choice and interleaving).
Space: exponential.

Limitation: completely infeasible at scale; decomposing into "max subsequence via monotonic stack" plus "greedy suffix-comparison merge" plus "try every split" reduces this to a polynomial-time solution.
8. Optimize the Solution

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why full enumeration is unnecessary: finding the best subsequence of a fixed length from a single array is a well-understood monotonic stack problem (identical in spirit to Remove K Digits), and merging two FIXED sequences greedily (by comparing full remaining suffixes) is provably optimal without needing to try every interleaving.

The monotonic stack subroutine: for array nums and target length len, scan left to right, popping a smaller digit off the stack whenever a larger one arrives AND enough digits remain to still reach length len, then truncate to length len.

The greedy merge subroutine: repeatedly compare the FULL remaining suffix of each sequence (not just their next digit), taking from whichever is lexicographically greater; this handles ties on the immediate next digit correctly by looking further ahead.

The split-search: since the split between the two arrays is unknown, try every valid split (i digits from nums1, k-i from nums2), applying the two subroutines above for each, and keep the best merged result across all splits.

For each valid split i (digits from nums1) and k-i (digits from nums2): extract the max subsequence of that length from each array via a monotonic stack, merge them greedily by comparing remaining suffixes, and track the best result across all splits.

blocks.caption: Monotonic stack for max subsequence per array; greedy suffix-comparison merge; try every split

blocks.text: Why This Works

The monotonic stack correctly finds the largest possible subsequence of a fixed length from a single array, using the same greedy "pop a smaller earlier digit if a larger one arrives and enough digits remain" logic as Remove K Digits. The greedy merge, by comparing FULL remaining suffixes (not just the next digit) at each step, correctly resolves ties on the immediate next digit by looking ahead, which is essential since taking from the wrong sequence on a tie could lead to a smaller overall result. Trying every valid split ensures the globally optimal division of k between the two arrays is found, since the best split cannot be determined without considering the resulting merge for each.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(k times (nums1.length + nums2.length) squared) roughly, due to trying every split and the O(n) suffix comparisons during merging, dominated by the merge step's repeated suffix comparisons.
Space: O(nums1.length + nums2.length) for each candidate merge.

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

Create Maximum Number is a hard problem combining three distinct techniques (monotonic-stack max subsequence, greedy suffix-comparison merge, and exhaustive split search) into one cohesive solution, a great test of composing multiple sub-algorithms correctly.
Common Mistakes

items: Comparing only the next single digit during the merge instead of the full remaining suffix, incorrectly breaking ties.
Forgetting to try ALL valid splits of k between the two arrays, potentially missing the globally optimal division.

blocks.text: Interview Tips

Explicitly decomposing this into the three named subroutines (max subsequence via monotonic stack, greedy suffix-comparison merge, exhaustive split search) before coding demonstrates strong problem decomposition skills for a genuinely hard combined problem.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "choose and merge subsequences from two sources to maximize a combined result", think: monotonic stack for the best subsequence per source, greedy suffix-comparison merge, and try every split.
Interview Follow-up Questions

items: How would you optimize the merge step further using suffix arrays for faster suffix comparisons?
How would this generalize to combining THREE or more source arrays?

blocks.text: Pattern Connections

items: Remove K Digits, the source of the monotonic-stack max-subsequence subroutine reused here.
Merge Two Sorted Lists and similar merge problems, though this greedy merge uniquely requires FULL suffix comparison, not just the next element.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: Full enumeration is exponential and infeasible; the combined monotonic-stack, greedy-merge, and split-search approach runs in polynomial time, the standard efficient solution for this hard problem.
12. Final Summary

items: Pattern: a three-part combination: monotonic-stack max subsequence per array, greedy suffix-comparison merge, and exhaustive split search.
Core Idea: for each valid split of k, extract the best subsequence of the required length from each array, merge them by comparing full remaining suffixes, and keep the best result across all splits.
Time: exponential for full enumeration, polynomial for the optimized combined approach.
Most Important Observation: merging must compare FULL remaining suffixes (not just the next digit) to correctly break ties.
Interview Difficulty: a genuinely hard problem, testing the ability to compose multiple distinct greedy subroutines correctly.
One line memory trick: monotonic stack per array, suffix-comparison merge, try every split.
